name: ephemeris
doc:
EPHEMERIS - the sky's calendar, sealed (issue #11, 2026-10-16: reach, down the domain list). Through
ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY: the Julian Day of J2000.0 and of the first Gregorian day; four eclipses sealed as the new
and full moons they must be; the four 2024 equinoxes and solstices to the day; sunrise and sunset for New York
on 2025-07-04 and for the equator at the equinox; and Kepler's third law in its gravitational form for the Earth,
a geostationary satellite, and the Moon - whose two-body period falls 0.14 percent short of the sidereal month,
the Sun's perturbation, kept as the method's stated bound. Meeus's algorithms are CITED at their stated
precision; the dates are SEALED. Idempotent.

sticks.question: Ephemeris - the sky's calendar, sealed
sticks.statement: Julian days, lunar phases, the equinoxes and solstices, sunrise and sunset, and orbital periods are closed-form functions of the date and the orbit.
references: J. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd ed. (1998), ch. 7, 25, 27, 49
NASA GSFC eclipse catalogue (F. Espenak): 2017-08-21, 2024-04-08 solar; 2019-01-21, 2022-11-08 lunar
J. Kepler, Harmonices Mundi (1619), Book V - the third law

marks.claim: [J2000.0, SEALED] 2000-01-01 at noon UT is Julian Day 2,451,545.0 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY; Meeus ch. 7) - the epoch every modern star catalogue is referred to. The Julian Day counts days since noon on 1 January 4713 BC (Scaliger 1583), a single integer line through every calendar.

[the first Gregorian day, SEALED] 1582-10-15, the day after 1582-10-04 in the reform, is JD 2,299,161.0 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY). Ten dates were skipped; the day count was not - which is why astronomers count days and not dates.

[the 2024 eclipse was a new moon, SEALED] 2024-04-08 - the total solar eclipse across North America - falls at the new moon (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY: mean lunar age within 1.5 d of 0). A solar eclipse is a new moon by definition: the Moon between us and the Sun.
[and 2017, SEALED] 2017-08-21, the 'Great American' eclipse, is a new moon (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY).

[a lunar eclipse is a full moon, SEALED] 2022-11-08, total lunar eclipse: full moon (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY). The Earth between Moon and Sun - the opposite configuration, half a synodic month from new.
[and 2019, SEALED] 2019-01-21, the total lunar eclipse: full moon (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY).
[the March equinox, SEALED] 2024-03-20 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY; USNO: 03:06 UT).
[the June solstice, SEALED] 2024-06-20 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY; USNO: 20:51 UT) - the earliest June solstice since 1796, the leap-cycle drift at its turn.
[the September equinox, SEALED] 2024-09-22 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY; USNO: 12:44 UT).

[the December solstice, SEALED] 2024-12-21 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY; USNO: 09:20 UT). Four dates a year the tilted Earth's orbit fixes; Meeus's Table 27 gives them to the day for a thousand years either way.

[sunrise in New York, SEALED] 2025-07-04 at 40.71 N, 74.01 W, EDT: sunrise 5:31 (5.52 h), sunset 8:31 pm (20.52 h) (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY, within the verifier's 0.5 h window; USNO gives 5:31 and 20:31). The geometry of a tilted axis, with refraction's 0.833 deg added to the horizon.

[the equator at the equinox, SEALED] 0 N, 0 E on 2024-03-20: sunrise 6:00, sunset 18:00 (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY). Equal night - with the refraction allowance the day runs about 12 h 7 min, which is why the date of truly equal day and night (the equilux) falls a few days before the equinox.
[Kepler's third law - the Earth, SEALED] a = 1.496e11 m about 1.989e30 kg: T = 2 pi sqrt(a^3 / G M) = 3.156e7 s, one year (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY, through G).

[the geostationary orbit, SEALED] a = 42,164 km about the Earth (5.9722e24 kg): T = 86,164 s, one sidereal day (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY). A satellite there hangs over one meridian - the orbit Clarke proposed in 1945, placed by Kepler's law and G.

[the Moon - the two-body period, SEALED] a = 384,400 km about Earth + Moon (6.0457e24 kg): T = 2.3574e6 s = 27.28 d (sealed through ephemeris.EPH_VERIFY). The observed sidereal month is 27.3217 d = 2.3606e6 s - 0.14 percent longer. The discordance is the Sun's pull on the Moon, which the two-body formula omits: it indicts the METHOD at that precision, not G or the distance. The honest number is sealed; the sidereal month is cited.

[the precision, CITED] Meeus's low-precision forms are used as stated: the equinox table without its periodic terms (good to about 2 days), the sunrise formula without the equation of time (about 0.5 h), the mean lunar age from a reference new moon (about 1.5 d). Each window is the stated precision and every claim above is judged at it; a claim finer than the method is declined, never waved through.
marks.source: J. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (1998) ch. 25, 27, 49; src/concordance/verifiers/ephemeris.py

marks.claim: [on the one map] The ephemeris is the calendar (card_floor_the_calendar: the Julian day line, the Gregorian reform) read off the orbits (card_floor_astronomy: phases, eclipses, the seasons) under gravity (Kepler's third law in Newton's form, through G). Everything here is time as the sky keeps it - the clock we are inside of.
marks.source: the one map; card_floor_the_calendar, card_floor_astronomy; the calendar stick
